items.title: Intro to HTML - What HTML Is
items.text: Goal: understand what HTML is, what it does, and how you write and save it,before you write your first page.

items.title: What is HTML?
items.text:
HTML = HyperText , Language.

  • HyperText: text that can link to other text. A page that can point to another page via links.
  • Markup: you mark up plain text with labels that say what each part is.
  • Language: a fixed set of labels (called tags) that every browser understands.

HTML is not a programming language. It has no logic, no variables, no if statements. It is a , language: it describes the structure and meaning of content.

items.title: What does HTML do?
items.text:
HTML tells the browser what things are, not what they look like.

<h1>Bakery</h1>
<p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
  • <h1>Bakery</h1>,"this is the main title of the page."
  • <p>Fresh bread daily.</p>,"this is a paragraph."

The browser then decides how to show that: big bold title, plain paragraph. Exact colours, fonts, and layout come later with CSS. Behaviour and interactivity come later with JavaScript.

Technology Job Example HTML Structure and meaning "This is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a link." CSS Looks and layout "Make the heading red and centred." JavaScript Behaviour "When clicked, show the menu."

This course covers HTML only. One core rule to carry with you: choose tags by meaning, never by looks.

items.title: Tags vs elements
items.text:
Beginners mix these up. They are different:

  • A tag is the label in angle brackets: <p>, </p>, <h1>.
  • An element is the whole unit: opening tag + content + closing tag.
An opening tag A closing tag

Most elements have both tags:

<h1>Bakery</h1>      <!-- opening <h1>, text, closing </h1> -->
<p>Fresh bread.</p>  <!-- opening <p>, text, closing </p> -->

A few elements have no content and no closing tag. These are called void (empty) elements:

<br>   <!-- line break -->
<hr>   <!-- horizontal rule -->
<img src="bread.jpg" alt="Loaf of bread">  <!-- image -->

items.title: Attributes
items.text:
Attributes provide additional information about the contents of an element. They appear on the opening tag of the element and are made up of two parts: a name and a value, separated by an equals sign.

A closing tag

The pattern to notice

Opening tags can carry extra info called attributes (like src and alt above). Closing tags never do. You will meet each attribute when its chapter arrives,for now just recognise the shape.

items.title: How HTML is stored, written, and saved
items.text:
1. HTML is plain text. No special software creates it. It is just characters in a file.
  2. You write it in a text editor,VS Code, Notepad, TextEdit, anything that saves plain text. Do not use Word or Google Docs: they add hidden formatting that breaks HTML.
  3. You save it with an .html ending, for example index.html. The .html tells the operating system and browser "read this as a webpage."
  4. You open it in a browser,double-click the file, or drag it into Chrome/Firefox/Edge. The browser reads the file top to bottom and draws the page.
you type (index.html)  →  browser reads  →  page you see
<h1>Bakery</h1>            understands        BIG TITLE
<p>Fresh bread.</p>        "title + para"     plain paragraph

Practical rules for this course:

  • Save every exercise as index.html in its own folder.
  • Always use UTF-8 encoding (your editor's default). This keeps characters like é, ñ, ü intact.
  • Name files in lowercase, no spaces: index.html, not My Page.HTML.
  • After every change: save the file, then refresh the browser. No save = no change on screen.

You do not need a server, the internet, or any build tool yet. A text file + a browser is the whole setup.

items.title: Try it: your first 3 lines
items.text:
1. Open your editor, create a new file.
  2. Type exactly this:
<h1>Bakery</h1>
<p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
  1. Save it as index.html.
  2. Open it in a browser.

You just wrote HTML: two elements, four tags, one title and one paragraph. Everything from here on is more labels for more kinds of content.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Idea Detail What HTML is HyperText , Language,labels for structure and meaning What it does Says what content is; browser renders it; CSS handles looks, JS handles behaviour Tag The bracketed label: <p>, </p> Element Whole unit: opening tag + content + closing tag (or a lone void element like <br>) How it lives Plain-text .html file, written in a code editor, opened in a browser

Next: Course Index,how the course is organised, then 01 - Basic Structure.

items.title: Basic HTML Course - Index
items.text: This is course material for HTML under the web development skilling program at Makerere High School Migadde.

items.title: How to study
items.text:
1. Read chapters in order,each one builds on the last.
  2. Type out every example in a file called index.html and open it in a browser.
  3. Chapters marked reference are detailed,skim first, return when you need exact syntax.

items.title: Chapters
items.text:
# Chapter What you learn 01 Basic Structure <!DOCTYPE>, <html>, <head>, <body>,the skeleton 02 What Are Headings? Why headings exist: outline, SEO, screen readers 03 Headings h1–h6 All six levels, the one-h1 rule, no skipped levels 04 What Are Paragraphs? Blocks of thought, p vs br, hr 05 Paragraphs, Breaks, Rules p, br, hr syntax in detail 06 Combined: Text in the Basic Structure h1 + p inside <body>,parent and children 07 Meaning vs Looks strong/b, em/i, mark,the go-semantic rule 08 Code Family code, kbd, samp, var 09 Tiny Semantics abbr, time, del/ins, sub/sup 10 Quotes blockquote, q, cite 11 Special Blocks pre, address, small 12 Links a, href, absolute/relative/anchor URLs 13 Images img, alt, figure/figcaption 14 Lists ul, ol, li, nesting, dl 15 Tables table, caption, thead/tbody, tr/th/td 16 Forms Basics form, label, input, button 17 Grouping: div, section, span div vs section, span, class/id hooks 18 Page Landmarks header, nav, main, footer, article, aside 19 Mini Project Build one complete page from spec

Next: 01,Basic Structure

items.title: 01 - Basic Structure of an HTML Page
items.text: Goal: understand the skeleton every webpage is built on: declaration first, then one root, then metadata, then visible content.

items.title: The full template
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Your Page Title</title>
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Your page content -->
</body>
</html>

Copy this to start every page. Read it top to bottom,order matters.

items.title: <!DOCTYPE html> - declaration, line 1
items.text:
• Declares the document as HTML5 so browsers render in standards mode (not quirks mode).
  • Not a tag,no closing tag, no attributes. Always the very first line, nothing above it.
<!DOCTYPE html>

items.title: <html> - root element, line 2
items.text:
• The parent of everything. Wraps <head> and <body>. Needs </html> as the last line.
  • lang sets the page language for SEO and screen readers:
<html lang="en">
lang value Meaning en English sw Swahili fr French

items.title: <head> - invisible metadata
items.text:
• Holds setup the visitor never sees on the page: <title>, <meta charset>, <meta viewport>, <link> to CSS, <script> to JS.
  • First child of <html>. Always before <body>.
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Bakery</title>
</head>
Tag inside <head> Job <title> Tab/window title + search-result title <meta charset="utf-8"> Character encoding,include always <meta name="viewport" …> Makes mobile browsers scale correctly,include always

items.title: <body> - visible content
items.text:
• Everything you see goes here: headings, paragraphs, lists, images, links, divs.
  • Second child of <html>. Exactly one <body> per page.
<body>
  <h1>Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
</body>
The struture of an HTML page

items.title: Hierarchy (who is inside who)
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>      declaration,comes first, owns nothing
<html>               PARENT,wraps all
  <head>             1st child,invisible setup
  <body>             2nd child,all visible content
  • <html> is the parent; <head> and <body> are its children.
  • <head> always before <body>. Nothing visible ever goes in <head> (except <title> on the tab).

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• One <!DOCTYPE>, one <html>, one <head>, one <body>,no more.
  • Close tags in reverse order: <html> opens second, closes last.
  • Forgetting <meta charset> can garble non-English characters. Forgetting viewport breaks mobile layout.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Order Tag Role 1st <!DOCTYPE html> Declaration 2nd <html lang> Root parent 3rd <head> Invisible metadata 4th <body> Visible content

Next: 02 - What Are Headings?

items.title: 02 - What Are Headings?
items.text: Goal: understand what headings are for before meeting all six levels.

items.title: Headings = the document outline
items.text:
Headings are section titles. Together they form the page's outline,the same way chapter titles outline a book:

<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
  • <h1> = the page's main title,exactly one per page.
  • <h2> = major sections. <h3>–<h6> = smaller and smaller subsections.

items.title: Meaning First -  size second
items.text:
Browsers draw <h1> biggest and <h6> smallest, with bold by default. But never pick a heading for its size:

  • Need small text? Use CSS, not <h4>.
  • Need big text? Use CSS, not <h1>.
  • Pick the level that describes the section's place in the outline.

items.title: Why headings matter beyond looks
items.text:
• Screen readers: blind users jump between headings to navigate. Skipping h1 → h3 confuses them,a level appears missing.
  • Search engines: h1/h2 text carries weight for what the page is about.
  • Skimmers: most visitors scan headings before reading anything.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
1. Exactly one <h1> per page.
  2. Never skip a level (h1 → h3, h2 → h4).
  3. Keep headings short and descriptive.
  4. Don't use headings to style non-heading text.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Idea Detail What Section titles forming the page outline Levels h1 (main) → h6 (deepest subsection) Pick by Meaning/position, never visual size Matters for Readers, screen readers, search engines

Next: 03 - Headings h1–h6 · Prev: 01 - Basic Structure

items.title: 03 - Headings h1–h6 Showcase
items.text: Goal: meet all six heading levels and see their relative sizes.

items.title: The rule first
items.text: There must be one <h1> per page. Never skip heading levels 1 to 3.

items.title: All six levels
items.text: Tag Renders (approx.) Use for <h1> Bakery Homepage (largest) Page title,once <h2> Our Menu Major sections <h3> Drinks Subsections <h4> Hot Drinks Sub-subsections <h5> Tea Notes Deep detail <h6> Fine print head (smallest) Rarely,deepest level

items.title: Snippets
items.text:
<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
<h3>Drinks</h3>
<h4>Hot Drinks</h4>
<h5>Tea Notes</h5>
<h6>Fine print head</h6>

A correctly nested example,note no skipped levels:

<h1>Bakery</h1>
<h2>Our Menu</h2>
<h3>Drinks</h3>
<h2>Prices</h2>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Two <h1> tags on one page: split the page or demote one to <h2>.
  • <h1> followed directly by <h3>: insert the missing <h2>, even if it feels redundant.
  • Styling a paragraph to look big is not a heading,screen readers won't list it.
Headings

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Level Size hint Role h1 Biggest Page title ×1 h2 Large Sections h3–h6 Shrinking Subsections, never skipped

Next: 04 - What Are Paragraphs? · Prev: 02 - What Are Headings?

items.title: 04 - What Are Paragraphs?
items.text: Goal: understand paragraphs as blocks of thought,and how br and hr differ.

items.title: Paragraphs = blocks of thought
items.text:
A paragraph groups sentences into one block, one idea. It is the default unit of web text:

<p>Fresh bread baked every morning.</p>
  • Block-level: each <p> starts on a new line, and browsers add space above and below automatically.
  • Readability: one idea per <p>. Short paragraphs scan far better on screens than walls of text.

items.title: <p> vs <br>
items.text:
• <p> = a new thought,a new block.
  • <br> = a line break inside the same thought,an address, a poem, a signature block:
<p>Line one<br>Line two, same thought</p>
Paragraphs

Never stack <br><br><br> to fake paragraph spacing. That is what <p> (and CSS margins) are for,stacked breaks mean nothing to screen readers.

items.title: <hr> = thematic break
items.text:
<hr> marks a scene change between blocks,a new scene in a story, menu switching to prices:

<p>Menu</p>
<hr>
<p>Prices</p>

It renders as a horizontal line, but its meaning is "the topic shifts here",it is not decoration.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
1. One idea per <p>; keep them short.
  2. <br> is an empty tag,no closing tag, use sparingly.
  3. <hr> is an empty tag,a topic shift, not a divider graphic.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Meaning Empty? p Block of thought No br Line break, same thought Yes hr Thematic break Yes

Next: 05 - Paragraphs, Breaks, Rules · Prev: 03 - Headings h1–h6

items.title: 05 - Paragraphs, Breaks, Rules (Syntax)
items.text: Goal: exact syntax for p, br, and hr.

items.title: <p> - paragraph
items.text:
Block of thought. Space above and below is automatic:

<p>Fresh bread baked daily.</p>

items.title: <br> - line break
items.text:
Empty tag,no closing tag. Breaks the line inside the same paragraph:

<p>Line one<br>Line two</p>

Renders as:

Line one Line two

items.title: <hr> - thematic break
items.text:
Empty tag,no closing tag. Topic shift between blocks:

<p>Menu</p>
<hr>
<p>Prices</p>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• <br> inside headings is occasionally fine (a two-line title), but never use it for vertical spacing,that is CSS's job.
  • Multiple <hr> in a row almost always means your sections need headings instead.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Closing tag? Job p Yes </p> Block of thought br No Line break, same thought hr No Thematic break

Next: 06 - Combined · Prev: 04 - What Are Paragraphs?

items.title: 06 - Combined: Headings + Paragraphs in the Basic Structure
items.text: Goal: see where text lives inside the skeleton from Chapter 01.

items.title: The same skeleton - now with text
items.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Bakery</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
</body>
</html>

items.title: Where each piece lives
items.text:
• <h1> and <p> live inside <body>,they are visible content.
  • <head> holds only <title> here, never visible text (the title shows on the browser tab).
  • <html> is the parent of both; <!DOCTYPE html> is the declaration above it all.

items.title: Why this matters
items.text:
• Text placed in <head> (outside <title>) will not render,a classic beginner bug.
  • Every chapter from here on adds tags that live in <body>, except page-level setup.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Zone Holds Visible? <head> <title>, <meta> No (tab title only) <body> h1–h6, p, everything in Ch. 07+ Yes

Next: 07 - Meaning vs Looks · Prev: 05 - Paragraphs, Breaks, Rules

items.title: 07 - Meaning vs Looks (The Core Rule)
items.text: Goal: learn the most important distinction in HTML text: semantic elements describe meaning; visual elements only change looks.

items.title: The rule
items.text:
When in doubt, go semantic,<strong> not <b>, <em> not <i>.

Semantic elements tell browsers, screen readers, and search engines what text means. Visual elements only change rendering.

items.title: <strong> - importance
items.text:
Renders bold and is announced as important by screen readers. Carries SEO weight:

<p>Warning: <strong>Do not enter.</strong></p>

items.title: <b> - visual bold only
items.text:
Looks bold. Means nothing to assistive tech or search:

<p>Use <b>bold</b> for looks alone.</p>

Prefer <strong> unless you explicitly mean "styling only" (e.g., a product name in a review).

items.title: <em> - emphasis
items.text:
Renders italic and is stressed by screen readers:

<p>We are <em>closed</em> today.</p>

items.title: <i> - visual italic only
items.text:
<p>The term <i>croissant</i> is French.</p>

Typical legitimate uses: foreign words, technical terms, transliterations. For stress, use <em>.

items.title: <mark> - highlighted passage
items.text:
Marks text as relevant,like a highlighter pen (default yellow background):

<p>Result: <mark>passed</mark></p>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Nesting is fine: <strong><em>both</em></strong>,close in reverse order.
  • <b>/<i> are not deprecated,they are just meaning-free. Use them rarely and deliberately.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Meaning? Renders strong Important Bold b None Bold em Emphasis Italic i None Italic mark Relevant/hit Highlighted

Next: 08 - Code Family · Prev: 06 - Combined

items.title: 08 - Code Family
items.text: Goal: mark up code, keyboard input, program output, and variables with meaning.

items.title: <code> - code fragment
items.text:
Inline code with code meaning (usually monospace). For multi-line blocks, wrap in <pre> (Chapter 11):

<p>Run <code>print(x)</code> to debug.</p>

items.title: <kbd> - keyboard input
items.text:
Keys the user must press. Put each key in its own tag:

<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save.</p>

items.title: <samp> - sample output
items.text:
Text a program produced:

<p>Output: <samp>Saved.</samp></p>

items.title: <var> - variable
items.text:
A math or programming variable (usually italic):

<p><var>x</var> = 5</p>

Combined example:

<p>Set <var>name</var> with <code>input()</code>, press <kbd>Enter</kbd>, expect <samp>Hello!</samp></p>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• <code> alone does not preserve line breaks,<pre><code>…</code></pre> does (see Chapter 11).
  • Don't use <var> for generic italics,that is <i> (or better, <em>).

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Means Example code Code fragment <code>print()</code> kbd Key to press <kbd>Enter</kbd> samp Program output <samp>Done.</samp> var Variable <var>x</var>

Next: 09 - Tiny Semantics · Prev: 07 - Meaning vs Looks

items.title: 09 - Tiny Semantics - Big Meaning
items.text: Goal: small inline tags that carry machine-readable meaning: abbreviations, dates, edits, formulas.

items.title: <abbr> - abbreviation
items.text:
title must hold the full form,shown as a tooltip and announced by screen readers:

<abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>

<abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr>

An <abbr> without title is pointless,never omit it.

items.title: <time>,date / time
items.text:
datetime holds the machine-readable value (ISO format); the content is the human reading:

<time datetime="2026-09-16">Sept 16, 2026</time>

<time datetime="07:00">7am</time>

Search engines and calendars can parse datetime,plain text they cannot.

items.title: <del> / <ins> - edits
items.text:
Deleted and inserted text. Browsers strike through <del> and underline <ins> with meaning (a document history, not decoration):

<del>Old price $5</del> <ins>New price $4</ins>

<p><del>closed</del> <ins>open</ins> on Sundays</p>

Optional cite (source URL) and datetime attributes record why/when:

<del cite="https://example.com/menu-v2" datetime="2026-09-01">Old menu</del>

items.title: <sub> / <sup> - subscript / superscript
items.text:
Formulas and footnotes,not generic small/raised styling:

<p>H<sub>2</sub>O and x<sup>2</sup></p>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• <del>/<ins> can wrap block content too (whole paragraphs), not just words.
  • For footnote markers pair <sup> with a matching link (Chapter 12).

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Key attribute Example abbr title (required in practice) <abbr title="…">HTML</abbr> time datetime (ISO) <time datetime="2026-09-16">…</time> del / ins cite, datetime (optional) <del>old</del> <ins>new</ins> sub / sup , H<sub>2</sub>O, x<sup>2</sup>

Next: 10 - Quotes · Prev: 08 - Code Family

items.title: 10 - Quotes: Block, Inline, Source
items.text: Goal: quote correctly with three tags, three jobs.

items.title: <blockquote> - long / block quote
items.text:
A standalone quoted passage. Browsers indent it. cite holds the source URL (not shown, but machine-readable):

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/interview">
  Fresh bread needs time, not shortcuts.
</blockquote>

items.title: <q> - short inline quote
items.text:
A quote inside a sentence. Browsers add the quotation marks for you,don't type them:

<p>She said <q>Stay hungry.</q></p>

Renders as: She said "Stay hungry."

items.title: <cite> - source title
items.text:
The title of the work quoted,a book, article, talk. Never a person's name on its own:

<cite>Whole Earth Catalog</cite>

Full pattern,quote plus its source:

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/catalog">
  <p>Stay hungry, stay foolish.</p>
  <footer>— <cite>Whole Earth Catalog</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• <q> inside <q> nests with alternating quote marks,browsers handle it.
  • cite the work, then name the author in plain text if needed: <cite>Book</cite> by A. Uthor.
  • cite attribute (on blockquote) = URL for machines. <cite> element = title for humans. Don't confuse them.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Job Marks added? blockquote Block quote Indent, no quotes q Inline quote Browser adds quotes cite Source title None

Next: 11 - Special Blocks · Prev: 09 - Tiny Semantics

items.title: 11 - Special Blocks
items.text: Goal: three block tags for exact whitespace, contact info, and fine print.

items.title: <pre> - preformatted text
items.text:
Keeps spaces and line breaks exactly as typed,the only element that does. The home of multi-line code:

<pre>line 1
  indented line 2</pre>

Pair with <code> for code blocks with meaning:

<pre><code>def hello():
    print("hi")</code></pre>

items.title: <address> - contact info
items.text:
Contact information for the page/section author or owner,not any postal address found in text:

<address>hello@mhsm.web<br>Dar es Salaam</address>

Browsers usually italicize it. It belongs near the footer or author bio.

items.title: <small> - fine print
items.text:
Side comments: copyright, disclaimers, legal notes, attributions:

<small>© 2026 MHSM. All rights reserved.</small>

Browsers render it one step smaller. It does not make text unimportant,only secondary.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Inside <pre>, you must still escape < as < or the browser reads it as a tag.
  • <address> must not contain headings or sectioning content,only contact lines.
  • <small> inside <footer> is the classic copyright pattern.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Job Watch out pre Exact whitespace Escape < as < address Author/owner contact Not any address small Fine print Still readable, not hidden

Next: 12 - Links · Prev: 10 - Quotes

items.title: 12 - Links
items.text: Goal: connect pages with <a>,the tag that makes the web a web.

items.title: The tag
items.text:
href holds the destination. The content is the link text,it must describe the destination:

<a href="https://example.com/menu">See our menu</a>

Never "click here",screen readers list links out of context, and search engines weigh link text.

items.title: Three kinds of destination
items.text:
<!-- absolute: another site -->
<a href="https://example.com">Example</a>

<!-- relative: your own site, same folder -->
<a href="menu.html">Menu</a>

<!-- relative: subfolder -->
<a href="docs/prices.html">Prices</a>

<!-- anchor: a spot on the same page -->
<a href="#prices">Jump to prices</a>
<h2 id="prices">Prices</h2>
Form Starts with Goes to Absolute https:// Another site Relative path, no scheme Your own site,portable across domains Anchor # Element with matching id on the page

items.title: Useful attributes
items.text:
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open in new tab</a>
Attribute Job href Destination (required) target="_blank" Open in a new tab,use rarely, warn the user rel="noopener" Security partner of target="_blank",always pair them title Extra hint,not a substitute for good link text

Special schemes:

<a href="mailto:hello@mhsm.web">Email us</a>
<a href="tel:+255700000000">Call us</a>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Relative links keep working when you move the whole site; absolute links to your own pages break that portability.
  • An <a> without href is not a link,keyboard users can't reach it.
  • Images can be links too: wrap <img> in <a> (Chapter 13), with meaningful alt.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Idea Rule Link text Describes destination, never "click here" Own pages Relative URLs New tabs Rarely, with rel="noopener" Anchors href="#id" ↔ id="id"

Next: 13 - Images · Prev: 11 - Special Blocks

items.title: 13 - Images
items.text: Goal: embed images accessibly with img,and caption them with figure.

items.title: The tag
items.text:
src is the file, alt is the text replacement. alt is effectively required,screen readers read it, search engines index it, and it shows when the image fails:

<img src="bread.jpg" alt="Fresh loaves on a wooden shelf">

items.title: Writing good alt
items.text: Image alt Informative photo Describe the content: "Fresh loaves on a wooden shelf" Decorative border Empty: alt="" so readers skip it Image link Describe the destination: alt="Our menu (PDF)", not "image"

items.title: Size and paths
items.text:
<img src="images/bread.jpg" alt="Fresh loaves" width="600">
  • src paths follow the same relative/absolute rules as links (Chapter 12).
  • width (and height) reserve layout space so the page doesn't jump while loading. Fine-tune display size with CSS later.

items.title: Captions with figure
items.text:
To attach a visible caption, wrap in <figure> with <figcaption>:

<figure>
  <img src="oven.jpg" alt="Baker sliding loaves into a stone oven">
  <figcaption>Morning bake, 5am.</figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption> must be the first or last child of <figure>.

items.title: Clickable images
items.text:
<a href="menu.html"><img src="menu-thumb.jpg" alt="Our menu"></a>

The alt describes where the link goes, not the pixels.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Never omit alt,validators flag it and readers suffer.
  • Huge photo files slow the page; resize before publishing (CSS can't shrink bytes).
  • title on images is not a substitute for alt.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Attribute/Tag Job src Image file path alt Text replacement,always present figure/figcaption Image + visible caption Linked <img> alt = link destination

Next: 14 - Lists · Prev: 12 - Links

items.title: 14 - Lists
items.text: Goal: structure related items with unordered, ordered, and description lists.

items.title: <ul> - unordered list
items.text:
Bulleted items, order doesn't matter. Each item is an <li>:

<ul>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
</ul>

items.title: <ol> - ordered list
items.text:
Numbered items, order matters,steps, rankings. Browsers number automatically:

<ol>
  <li>Mix flour and water.</li>
  <li>Knead ten minutes.</li>
  <li>Bake at 220°C.</li>
</ol>

Start numbering elsewhere with start, reverse with reversed:

<ol start="5">
  <li>Fifth step first</li>
</ol>

items.title: Nesting lists
items.text:
An <li> can hold a whole sub-list,the nested list goes inside the <li>, not after it:

<ul>
  <li>Bread
    <ul>
      <li>White</li>
      <li>Brown</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Milk</li>
</ul>

items.title: <dl> - description list
items.text:
Term/definition pairs,glossaries, menus with descriptions, metadata:

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>HyperText Markup Language,page structure.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Cascading Style Sheets,page styling.</dd>
</dl>
Tag Job dl The whole description list dt Term dd Definition/description

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Only <li> may be a direct child of ul/ol,no bare text or <p> wrappers at that level.
  • Don't fake lists with <br> or - dashes; readers lose the count and structure.
  • Navigation menus are lists too (<nav><ul>…),you'll meet this pattern constantly.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
List Use when Markers ul Order irrelevant Bullets ol Order matters Numbers (auto) dl Term → definition None

Next: 15 - Tables · Prev: 13 - Images

items.title: 15 - Tables
items.text:
Goal: present true tabular data with table,rows, headers, and captions.

Tables are for data (prices, schedules). Never use them for page layout,that era ended.

items.title: Minimal table
items.text:
<table>
  <caption>Morning prices</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Item</th>
      <th scope="col">Price</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Bread</td>
      <td>$1</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Milk</td>
      <td>$2</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

items.title: Tag reference
Rules
items.text:
• Every row should end up with the same effective column count,mismatches render ragged.
  • th without scope still works visually but leaves screen-reader users guessing.
  • Styling (borders, striping) belongs to CSS,keep markup structural.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Piece Rule caption Always,names the table thead/tbody Group header vs data rows th + scope Label columns/rows for readers tr Contains only th/td

Next: 16 - Forms Basics · Prev: 14 - Lists

items.title: 16 - Forms Basics
items.text: Goal: collect user input with form, label, input, and button.

items.title: Minimal form
items.text:
<form action="/order" method="post">
  <label for="name">Name:</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
  <button type="submit">Order</button>
</form>
Piece Job form Groups inputs; action = where data goes, method = get or post label Names an input,for must match the input's id input The field itself,type picks its behavior button type="submit" Sends the form

items.title: Common input types
items.text:
<label for="mail">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="mail" name="mail" required>

<label for="qty">Loaves:</label>
<input type="number" id="qty" name="qty" min="1" max="12" value="1">

<label for="day">Pickup day:</label>
<input type="date" id="day" name="day">

<label for="note">Note:</label>
<textarea id="note" name="note" rows="3"></textarea>

<label><input type="checkbox" name="sliced"> Sliced</label>
type Collects Notes text Short text Default type email Email address Browser validates format number Number min/max/step constrain date Calendar date ISO value YYYY-MM-DD checkbox On/off Label wrapping is fine

required blocks empty submission; name is the key the server receives,an input without name sends nothing.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Clicking a <label> focuses its input,if it doesn't, your for/id mismatch.
  • method="get" puts data in the URL (searchable/shareable); post hides it in the request (orders, logins).
  • Never trust browser validation alone,servers must re-check everything.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Rule Detail Label everything for ↔ id, always Name everything No name = no data sent Submit <button type="submit">, not a link

Next: 17 - Grouping · Prev: 15 - Tables

items.title: 17 - Grouping: div, section, span
items.text: Goal: group content with div (generic), section (thematic), and span (inline).

items.title: The problem
items.text:
So far every tag describes one thing: a heading, a paragraph, a list item. Real pages need containers,boxes that hold several tags together so you can move, style, or name them as a unit:

<h2>Our Menu</h2>
<ul>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li>Milk</li>
</ul>
<h2>Prices</h2>
<table>…</table>

Which parts belong together? Without containers, CSS and screen readers see one flat list. div and section fix that.

items.title: <div> - generic block container
items.text:
A block-level box with no meaning. Use it to group things for styling or scripting:

<div class="card">
  <h2>Bread</h2>
  <p>Fresh daily.</p>
</div>
  • class names the group for CSS ("card" can repeat on many boxes).
  • id names one unique box on the page (id="prices" can appear only once, and links can jump to it: <a href="#prices">).
<div id="prices">
  <h2>Prices</h2>
  <p>Updated weekly.</p>
</div>

items.title: <section> - thematic group
items.text:
A section is a div with meaning: a themed chunk of the page,like a chapter in a book. Rule: every <section> needs a heading (h1–h6) as its first child:

<section>
  <h2>Our Menu</h2>
  <ul>
    <li>Bread</li>
    <li>Milk</li>
  </ul>
</section>

No heading? Use <div>,not <section>:

<!-- Wrong: section with no heading -->
<section>
  <p>Just a styled box.</p>
</section>

<!-- Right: generic box -->
<div class="notice">
  <p>Just a styled box.</p>
</div>

items.title: <span> - inline div
items.text:
span is to inline content what div is to block content: a meaning-free wrapper inside a sentence:

<p>Result: <span class="price">$1</span></p>
Container Block or inline? Meaning? Rule div Block None Group for styling/scripting section Block Thematic group Must contain a heading span Inline None Never wrap whole paragraphs

items.title: Decision rule
items.text:
Need a wrapper?
  ├─ Themed chunk with a heading? → <section>
  ├─ Inside a sentence/word?      → <span>
  └─ Otherwise (styling hook)?    → <div>

items.title: Nesting
items.text:
Containers nest,inner closes before outer,like all HTML:

<section>
  <h2>Our Menu</h2>
  <div class="card">
    <h3>Bread</h3>
    <p>Price: <span class="price">$1</span></p>
  </div>
</section>

<section>          thematic group
  <h2>             its heading,required
  <div>            generic box inside
    <h3> + <p>    visible content
    <span>         inline hook inside <p>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Don't use div where a precise tag fits: a list of items is <ul>,not <div>s; tabular data is <table>,not <div>s.
  • Don't wrap every single element in a div,group things that belong together,extra boxes add noise for readers and CSS.
  • id values must be unique per page; class values may repeat.
  • <div> cannot go inside <p>,the browser will close the paragraph early. <span> can.

items.title: Recap
items.text:
Tag Job Watch out div Generic block group No meaning, needs class/id to be useful section Themed group Must have a heading, else use div span Generic inline group Inside sentences only

Next: 18 - Page Landmarks · Prev: 16 - Forms Basics

items.title: 18 - Page Landmarks: header, nav, main, footer, article, aside
items.text: Goal: build a full page skeleton with landmark tags screen readers and search engines understand.

items.title: Why not only div?
items.text:
Chapter 17 gave you generic boxes. This page uses only them:

<div id="header">
  <div class="nav">…</div>
</div>
<div id="main">…</div>
<div id="footer">…</div>

It renders fine, but assistive tech sees three identical boxes. Landmark tags say what each box is:

<header>…</header>
<nav>…</nav>
<main>…</main>
<footer>…</footer>

Screen-reader users jump straight to <nav> or <main>; search engines weigh <main> content highest.

items.title: <header> - intro of page or section
items.text:
Page banner (logo, title) or the intro of a section/article. Not one-per-page,one per scope:

<header>
  <h1>Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread daily.</p>
</header>

items.title: <nav> - major navigation
items.text:
Wraps the main menu,almost always a list (Chapter 14 pattern):

<nav>
  <ul>
    <li><a href="#menu">Menu</a></li>
    <li><a href="#prices">Prices</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

Use nav only for major navigation (site menu, table of contents),not every link group.

items.title: <main> - the page's core
items.text:
The unique central content. Rules: exactly one per page, never nested inside header/footer/nav:

<main>
  <section>
    <h2>Our Menu</h2>
    <p>…</p>
  </section>
</main>

items.title: <footer> - closing of page or section
items.text:
Author info, copyright, contact (pairs with <address> and <small> from Chapter 11):

<footer>
  <address>hello@mhsm.web</address>
  <small>© 2026 MHSM. All rights reserved.</small>
</footer>

items.title: <article> vs <section> vs <aside>
Full skeleton
items.text:
Chapters 01 + 17 + 18 together:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Bakery</title>
</head>
<body>
  <header>
    <h1>Bakery</h1>
    <nav>
      <ul>
        <li><a href="#menu">Menu</a></li>
        <li><a href="#prices">Prices</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>
  <main>
    <section>
      <h2 id="menu">Our Menu</h2>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Bread</h3>
        <p>Fresh daily.</p>
      </div>
    </section>
    <section>
      <h2 id="prices">Prices</h2>
      <p>Updated weekly.</p>
    </section>
  </main>
  <footer>
    <address>hello@mhsm.web</address>
    <small>© 2026 MHSM. All rights reserved.</small>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• One <main> per page. Extra mains confuse navigation ("which one is the content?").
  • Don't put <main> inside <header>, <footer>, or <nav>,it must be a top-level zone of <body>.
  • header/footer inside an article/section belong to that block,not the whole page.
  • Don't fake landmarks with <div id="header">,same rendering, zero meaning.

items.title: Recap
items.text: Tag Job Rule header Intro/banner Per page or per section/article nav Major navigation Wraps a list, not every link main Core content Exactly one, top-level in body footer Closing/contact Pairs with address + small article Standalone piece Must make sense on its own aside Tangential box Sidebar, tip, related links
